paragraphs: We are a local building firm, based just three miles away in Sawbridgeworth, and Bishop's Stortford is very much our home patch. We design and build house extensions across the town and its villages, from a rear extension on a period home near the centre to a larger project on one of the newer estates, and we run the whole job as one team, from the first visit through design, planning and building regulations to the finished room.

This is a town people work hard to stay in, an old malting town on the Stort with fast trains to London and good schools. So the work here is usually about making a home you love bigger and better rather than moving away from it.

planning.title: Planning permission in Bishop's Stortford
paragraphs: Here is the local detail that catches people out, and it is worth knowing before you plan anything.

Your planning authority is East Hertfordshire District Council. The town-centre conservation area is covered by an Article 4 direction, confirmed in 2017, which removes a number of the permitted development rights you would normally have. In practice that means around 1,500 households need planning permission for things that are automatic elsewhere, including some window and door changes, roof coverings and street-facing alterations. Most work that is not visible from the street, and genuine like-for-like repairs, are generally not affected, but it pays to check. Listed buildings, of which the old town has many, need separate consent.

Out on the newer estates it is a different story, and many extensions there still fall under permitted development. Knowing which regime your home sits under is exactly where we start, so you do not design something that was never going to be allowed. One note for the future: East Herts is due to be replaced by a new unitary council around 2028, though the rules will carry over. We check where your property stands and manage any application for you.

The ground here is boulder clay over London Clay, the stiff glacial clay that blankets this part of the Hertfordshire and Essex border, with the River Stort valley cutting through the town. Boulder clay is generally firm but variable, and the London Clay beneath swells and shrinks with the seasons, moving most near mature trees. Closer to the Stort the ground can be softer and wetter, with a higher water table.

On a plot near a large tree, or down towards the river, foundations often need more depth and thought than people expect. We would rather design for that from the start than meet it as a surprise, so on trickier plots we get the ground checked before pricing the groundworks.

cost.title: What an extension costs in Bishop's Stortford
paragraphs: Cost comes down to size, specification, structural work and finish, and heritage work in the conservation area can add to it.

As a general guide, single-storey extensions commonly run at a few thousand pounds per square metre of finished space, with double storey often better value per square metre. faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for an extension in Bishop's Stortford?
faqs.a: It depends where your home is. In the town-centre conservation area, an Article 4 direction means more work needs permission than usual, including some window, door and street-facing changes. On the newer estates, many extensions fall under permitted development. We check your exact address with East Herts District Council and handle any application.

faqs.q: What does the Article 4 direction mean for my home?
faqs.a: If your property is in the conservation area, some changes that would normally be automatic now need planning permission, mainly ones visible from the street. Work hidden from public view and genuine like-for-like repairs are usually unaffected. We will tell you exactly how it applies to your house.

faqs.q: How do I get a quote for my extension?
faqs.a: Call us on 07920 731533 or send the enquiry form. We arrange a free, no-obligation site visit, then give you a clear, itemised written quote for the actual project.

faqs.q: Is the first visit really free and no-obligation?
faqs.a: Yes. The visit and the quote cost nothing, and there is no pressure to proceed.

faqs.q: Why does the local ground matter for my foundations?
faqs.a: Bishop's Stortford sits on boulder clay over London Clay, which moves with the seasons and near trees, and the ground softens towards the Stort valley. That often means deeper or specially designed foundations, so we check the ground before starting.

faqs.q: Which areas around Bishop's Stortford do you cover?
faqs.a: Bishop's Stortford itself, along with Sawbridgeworth, Stansted, Much Hadham, Thorley and the surrounding villages, and we are based right nearby. Call us to confirm your postcode.

buildProcess.title: What the build actually looks like
buildProcess.text: Once we are on site, a single-storey extension usually runs roughly like this, allowing for size, weather and ground: Weeks 1 to 2: setting up, then groundworks and foundations. Weeks 3 to 4: brickwork to damp-proof course, drainage and the slab. Weeks 4 to 6: walls up, structural steel in, roof on and watertight. Weeks 6 to 8: windows and doors, first-fix electrics and plumbing. Weeks 8 to 10: plastering, second fix and the kitchen fit-out. Final week: decorating, flooring and snagging before we hand over.
